3 models · VBVR-CustomEval · identical SFT recipe, identical 4,500-row training set, identical 900-sample eval

Does starting from a bigger next-frame checkpoint help?

All three models were fine-tuned with the exact same recipe (LoRA rank 32 on the LLM, lr 1e-5, batch 16, no-ce / image-loss-only supervision, all conditioning images through the ViT) on the same new 4,500-row training set — 9 tasks × 500 rows each (the 5 ID tasks subsampled from their existing 2,000-row pool; the 4 OOD tasks freshly generated for this run, since they'd never had a train split before). The only difference is the starting checkpoint: one run starts from the InternVL-U base model, one continues from the checkpoint fine-tuned on 100,000 VBVR next-frame rows, and the third continues from a checkpoint fine-tuned on 140,000 next-frame rows (the same 100k plus 40,000 freshly-generated rows for the 4 tasks that used to be held out as OOD, now folded in as ordinary training data). All three are evaluated on the identical 900-sample (9 task × 100), 9-task target-frame-prediction eval split, scored twice: once by a deterministic rule-based detector pipeline, once by a Qwen3-VL-30B-fp8 judge.

Rule-based method

Per task, a small set of weighted sub-criteria (e.g. for stable_sort: classification, order, fidelity, layout) is computed from classical computer vision — contour detection, HSV color masks, connected-component analysis — identically for both models' outputs. Deterministic, zero marginal cost per sample.

Judge method

A Qwen3-VL-30B-fp8 judge is shown the same three images (starting frame, candidate, ground truth) and classifies each sub-criterion into wrong partial correct (0 / 0.5 / 1.0), combined with the identical weights the rule-based side uses.

Second judge — Qwen3.8-27B

Added 2026-08-31: the identical rubric/instruction/weights, but asked of Qwen3.8-27B (a brand-new hybrid-linear-attention VL model) instead, run locally via transformers rather than vLLM — vLLM itself cannot currently serve this checkpoint on this cluster (community INT4 quant crashes a Marlin kernel; official bf16's tensor-parallel path needs CUDA-13-only compiled extensions this cluster's driver can't run). Scored on the same 10–20-sample subset shown below, not the full 900/task pool — see the caveat box further down.

Knowledge ID

ball_bounces_given_time

A ball starts at a marked position with a direction arrow, and is supposed to bounce off the boundary walls a stated number of times following elastic collision physics (angle of incidence = angle of reflection), ending at a specific final position. Note: this scene shows only the ball's resting position, not a drawn bounce path -- you cannot verify bounce count or reflection angles from a single static image, only final position.

Rule-based method

Single criterion: distance between the ball's detected final position and the ground truth's, via Hough-circle / dark-blob detection.

final_position100%
correctThe ball's final position in the candidate is essentially the same location as in the ground truth (small pixel offset, clearly the same resting spot).
partialThe ball is in roughly the right region/quadrant of the frame but noticeably off from the exact ground-truth position.
wrongThe ball is in a clearly different location, missing entirely, or the scene doesn't show a plausible resting ball at all.

Judge method — exact prompt sent

You are a strict, deterministic grader for a visual reasoning benchmark. You will see three images in order: (1) the starting frame, (2) a candidate generated result, (3) the ground-truth correct result. Judge ONLY image (2) against the rubric below, using image (3) as the reference for what 'correct' looks like and image (1) for the scene before the task was applied.

Verify each criterion against the actual pixel content of image (2), not against what the task instruction merely asks for -- a model that fails the task often still uses the right colors, shapes, or object count, just in the wrong positions. Do not mark a criterion 'correct' because the right elements appear SOMEWHERE in the image; their exact positions, alignment, and completeness must specifically match image (3). For anything laid out on a grid or along a path, compare element-by-element (cell by cell, or step by step) against image (3) rather than forming a general impression of similarity -- if you cannot point to the specific matching detail, do not call it correct. A candidate that is mostly blank, or where the drawn content covers only a small fraction of what a complete result should show (e.g. a short stub instead of a full path), is wrong or at best partial, never correct, even if the fragment that is there looks locally clean.

Task: A ball starts at a marked position with a direction arrow, and is supposed to bounce off the boundary walls a stated number of times following elastic collision physics (angle of incidence = angle of reflection), ending at a specific final position. Note: this scene shows only the ball's resting position, not a drawn bounce path -- you cannot verify bounce count or reflection angles from a single static image, only final position.

Task instruction given to the generator: "Generate a single image showing the final result of the task described below. Do not produce a video, animation, sequence of frames, or intermediate steps — output one image representing the completed final state only.

Task: A ball is placed at the initial position with a direction arrow indicating its movement direction. The ball bounces 5 times off the boundary walls following elastic collision physics (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection). Show its final position after the 5th bounce -- at the wall where the last collision occurs -- with its complete path drawn from start to end."

For EACH criterion below, classify the candidate into exactly one of three levels -- wrong, partial, or correct -- using the concrete definition given for that level (do not use a finer-grained number; pick the closest of the three):

- final_position:
    correct: The ball's final position in the candidate is essentially the same location as in the ground truth (small pixel offset, clearly the same resting spot).
    partial: The ball is in roughly the right region/quadrant of the frame but noticeably off from the exact ground-truth position.
    wrong: The ball is in a clearly different location, missing entirely, or the scene doesn't show a plausible resting ball at all.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no other text: {"criteria": {"final_position": "correct"|"partial"|"wrong"}, "reasoning": "<one or two short sentences>"}

Perception ID

stable_sort

Shapes of two types, each in three sizes, start scattered. They must be rearranged into a single horizontal line: grouped by type, and within each group ordered smallest-to-largest left to right.

Rule-based method

Contour-based shape detection (type/size/color/position) recovers each shape; classification, order, fidelity, and layout are checked against the sorted target arrangement.

classification30%
correctAll shapes of the same type are grouped adjacent to each other with no type intermixed.
partialMost shapes are grouped by type but one or two are out of place, or a group is split.
wrongShapes of different types are scattered/interleaved with no type grouping.
order30%
correctWithin every type-group, shapes run smallest-to-largest left to right.
partialSome groups are correctly ordered by size, others are not, or order is only partially correct within a group.
wrongShapes within groups are not ordered by size at all (random or reversed).
fidelity30%
correctEvery shape's type, size, and color exactly matches the first frame -- nothing added, removed, or recolored.
partialMost shapes match the first frame but one shape's color/size/type looks altered or minorly distorted.
wrongShapes were added, removed, or multiple shapes changed type/color/size from the first frame.
layout10%
correctAll shapes sit on the same horizontal line (baseline).
partialMost shapes are roughly aligned but a few are noticeably off the line.
wrongShapes are scattered at clearly different heights, not in a line.

Judge method — exact prompt sent

You are a strict, deterministic grader for a visual reasoning benchmark. You will see three images in order: (1) the starting frame, (2) a candidate generated result, (3) the ground-truth correct result. Judge ONLY image (2) against the rubric below, using image (3) as the reference for what 'correct' looks like and image (1) for the scene before the task was applied.

Verify each criterion against the actual pixel content of image (2), not against what the task instruction merely asks for -- a model that fails the task often still uses the right colors, shapes, or object count, just in the wrong positions. Do not mark a criterion 'correct' because the right elements appear SOMEWHERE in the image; their exact positions, alignment, and completeness must specifically match image (3). For anything laid out on a grid or along a path, compare element-by-element (cell by cell, or step by step) against image (3) rather than forming a general impression of similarity -- if you cannot point to the specific matching detail, do not call it correct. A candidate that is mostly blank, or where the drawn content covers only a small fraction of what a complete result should show (e.g. a short stub instead of a full path), is wrong or at best partial, never correct, even if the fragment that is there looks locally clean.

Task: Shapes of two types, each in three sizes, start scattered. They must be rearranged into a single horizontal line: grouped by type, and within each group ordered smallest-to-largest left to right.

Task instruction given to the generator: "Generate a single image showing the final result of the task described below. Do not produce a video, animation, sequence of frames, or intermediate steps — output one image representing the completed final state only.

Task: The scene contains two types of shapes, each type has three shapes of different sizes arranged randomly. Keep all shapes unchanged in appearance (type, size, and color). Only rearrange their positions: first group the shapes by type, then within each group, sort the shapes from smallest to largest (left to right), and arrange all shapes in a single horizontal line from left to right."

For EACH criterion below, classify the candidate into exactly one of three levels -- wrong, partial, or correct -- using the concrete definition given for that level (do not use a finer-grained number; pick the closest of the three):

- classification:
    correct: All shapes of the same type are grouped adjacent to each other with no type intermixed.
    partial: Most shapes are grouped by type but one or two are out of place, or a group is split.
    wrong: Shapes of different types are scattered/interleaved with no type grouping.
- order:
    correct: Within every type-group, shapes run smallest-to-largest left to right.
    partial: Some groups are correctly ordered by size, others are not, or order is only partially correct within a group.
    wrong: Shapes within groups are not ordered by size at all (random or reversed).
- fidelity:
    correct: Every shape's type, size, and color exactly matches the first frame -- nothing added, removed, or recolored.
    partial: Most shapes match the first frame but one shape's color/size/type looks altered or minorly distorted.
    wrong: Shapes were added, removed, or multiple shapes changed type/color/size from the first frame.
- layout:
    correct: All shapes sit on the same horizontal line (baseline).
    partial: Most shapes are roughly aligned but a few are noticeably off the line.
    wrong: Shapes are scattered at clearly different heights, not in a line.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no other text: {"criteria": {"classification": "correct"|"partial"|"wrong", "order": "correct"|"partial"|"wrong", "fidelity": "correct"|"partial"|"wrong", "layout": "correct"|"partial"|"wrong"}, "reasoning": "<one or two short sentences>"}

shape_color_then_move

A top row of 3 reference shapes (A, B, C) demonstrates a color-then-move transform pattern. The bottom row keeps shape D fixed and must add two new shapes E, F colored like B, following the same pattern.

Rule-based method

Per-shape detection (type/color/position) on both frames checks the untouched reference row stayed pixel-identical, then whether the pattern was correctly completed.

first_row_preservation40%
correctAll three top-row reference shapes are pixel-identical to the first frame -- completely untouched.
partialTop-row shapes are mostly unchanged but one looks slightly altered (color/position/size).
wrongTop-row reference shapes are noticeably changed, moved, or missing.
second_row_completion35%
correctBottom row keeps D in place and adds exactly two new shapes E and F alongside it.
partialBottom row has D plus some new shapes, but the count is off (only one added, or extra shapes), or D moved slightly.
wrongBottom row does not follow the pattern at all -- D missing/moved, or no new shapes added correctly.
color_accuracy20%
correctE and F are colored to match reference shape B specifically.
partialE and F have some correct coloring but one is the wrong color, or the match is approximate.
wrongE and F are colored incorrectly, not matching B at all.
shape_count5%
correctExactly 6 shapes total in the final image (3 top + 3 bottom).
partialClose to 6 shapes (off by one).
wrongShape count is clearly wrong (missing multiple or many extra shapes).

Judge method — exact prompt sent

You are a strict, deterministic grader for a visual reasoning benchmark. You will see three images in order: (1) the starting frame, (2) a candidate generated result, (3) the ground-truth correct result. Judge ONLY image (2) against the rubric below, using image (3) as the reference for what 'correct' looks like and image (1) for the scene before the task was applied.

Verify each criterion against the actual pixel content of image (2), not against what the task instruction merely asks for -- a model that fails the task often still uses the right colors, shapes, or object count, just in the wrong positions. Do not mark a criterion 'correct' because the right elements appear SOMEWHERE in the image; their exact positions, alignment, and completeness must specifically match image (3). For anything laid out on a grid or along a path, compare element-by-element (cell by cell, or step by step) against image (3) rather than forming a general impression of similarity -- if you cannot point to the specific matching detail, do not call it correct. A candidate that is mostly blank, or where the drawn content covers only a small fraction of what a complete result should show (e.g. a short stub instead of a full path), is wrong or at best partial, never correct, even if the fragment that is there looks locally clean.

alignment30%

fidelity20%

correctAll animals from the first frame are present in the final arrangement.
partialMost animals are present but one is missing or an extra one appears.
wrongMultiple animals are missing from the final arrangement.

Spatiality OOD

maze

An agent must navigate a maze from a green start marker to a red end marker, drawing its path through the maze.

Rule-based method

Orange/yellow path-marker mask vs. black wall mask checks the drawn path never crosses a wall, reaches both markers, moves only between adjacent cells, and the maze itself is untouched. Gated by a path-coverage check (drawn path pixels vs. the GT's own path pixel count) so short stubs that never reach the end can't score as if they were a full solve.

path_validity45%
correctThe drawn path stays entirely within corridors and never crosses a wall.
partialThe path is mostly valid but crosses a wall or cuts a corner in one spot.
wrongThe path crosses walls repeatedly or doesn't follow the maze corridors at all.
path_completeness30%
correctThe drawn path fully connects the start to the end marker with no gaps.
partialThe path covers most of the route but has a gap or doesn't quite reach the end.
wrongThe path is fragmented, very incomplete, or doesn't connect start and end at all.
navigation_accuracy20%
correctThe path moves only between adjacent cells, no jumps or teleports.
partialMostly adjacent-cell moves but one jump/teleport is visible.
wrongThe path makes multiple jumps that skip cells or teleport across the maze.
element_preservation5%
correctMaze walls and start/end markers are unchanged from the first frame.
partialWalls/markers are mostly unchanged but something looks slightly altered.
wrongWalls or markers are clearly changed, missing, or redrawn differently.

Judge method — exact prompt sent

You are a strict, deterministic grader for a visual reasoning benchmark. You will see three images in order: (1) the starting frame, (2) a candidate generated result, (3) the ground-truth correct result. Judge ONLY image (2) against the rubric below, using image (3) as the reference for what 'correct' looks like and image (1) for the scene before the task was applied.

Verify each criterion against the actual pixel content of image (2), not against what the task instruction merely asks for -- a model that fails the task often still uses the right colors, shapes, or object count, just in the wrong positions. Do not mark a criterion 'correct' because the right elements appear SOMEWHERE in the image; their exact positions, alignment, and completeness must specifically match image (3). For anything laid out on a grid or along a path, compare element-by-element (cell by cell, or step by step) against image (3) rather than forming a general impression of similarity -- if you cannot point to the specific matching detail, do not call it correct. A candidate that is mostly blank, or where the drawn content covers only a small fraction of what a complete result should show (e.g. a short stub instead of a full path), is wrong or at best partial, never correct, even if the fragment that is there looks locally clean.

How this comparison was built

A step-by-step log of the sessions that produced this report — what was done, the exact paths/commands, and why each step was necessary — kept here so the same SFT comparison can be reproduced (or extended to a further checkpoint) without re-deriving any of it. Phases 01-08 are the original 2-model (frombase/from100k) build; phase 09 documents the from140k addition.

01

Scope the eval set: which tasks are actually active

evaluators/image_evaluator.py's LOCKED_TASKS names 10 tasks (5 ID + 5 OOD) as the ones actually used for InternVL-U training/eval, out of 15 implemented evaluator classes. Of those 10, only 9 have real generations/eval data: glass_refraction (Knowledge, OOD) has no eval split because its DataFactory generator repo is access-restricted. The 9 active tasks:

  • ID (5, has a training split): ball_bounces_given_time, grid_shift, multi_object_placement, rotation_puzzle, stable_sort
  • OOD (4, had no training split until this session): shape_color_then_move, animal_size_sorting, maze, 2d_geometric_transformation

Two training-data pools exist for the ID tasks, from two independent pipelines: data/vbvr_next_frame/next_frame_train.jsonl (10 tasks × 10,000 rows, 3-frame-in → 1-out, used for the earlier 100k-row baseline) and data/vbvr_target_pred_id/target_pred_id_train.jsonl (5 of those tasks × 2,000 rows, 1-frame-in → 1-out — the task type this report is about). The OOD tasks had zero rows in either pool.

02

Generate the missing OOD training data

Ran each OOD task's own DataFactory generator for 500 new samples/task, into a new output directory with a new seed — both deliberate, to avoid corrupting the existing 100-sample eval split:

python VBVR-DataGeneration/target_pred/vbvr_target_pred_generate_ood_train.py # -> TASKS_OOD, seed=342, out_dir=/scratch/network/ssd/junlin/vbvr_target_pred/ood_train500/{task}/raw # (existing eval split: seed=242, out_dir=.../ood/{task}/raw -- untouched)
Why a new seed and a new directory, not just a bigger --num-raw on the existing one: the generator's generate_dataset() always numbers samples {domain}_{i:08d} starting at i=0, so re-running it against the same output directory overwrites whatever was already there. Reusing seed 242 with a larger count risks the first 100 draws colliding with the already-scored eval set; a disjoint seed (342, following the project's 142=ID/242=OOD-eval pattern) into a disjoint directory (ood_train500/ not ood/) guarantees zero overlap by construction, verified afterward by diffing image paths between the two jsonls (0 overlap).

Built the jsonl for that raw data with a small new script that reuses the project's existing build_rows() (prompt-wrapping, video-language audit) but writes split="train" to a new file instead of overwriting the eval jsonl:

python VBVR-DataGeneration/target_pred/vbvr_target_pred_build_ood_train.py # -> data/vbvr_target_pred_ood/target_pred_ood_train.jsonl (2,000 rows: 4 tasks x 500)
03

Assemble the final 4,500-row training set

For the 5 ID tasks, subsampled 500/task (fixed per-task seed tp_9task_subsample:{task}) out of the existing 2,000-row train pool. For the 4 OOD tasks, used all 500 freshly generated rows. Every row was then converted to the no_ce format — a top-level "no_ce": true field plus collapsing the gpt turn from a templated sentence to the bare <img> marker — to match how the earlier 100k-row baseline was trained (confirmed by diffing that run's with-CE vs no-CE jsonls beforehand; the two default-built jsonls here had never been converted).

python VBVR-DataGeneration/target_pred/vbvr_target_pred_merge_9task.py # -> data/vbvr_target_pred_9task/target_pred_9task_train_no_ce.jsonl (4,500 rows) # -> data/meta/vbvr_target_pred_9task_meta.json
Why no_ce matters here: VBVR prompts are synthesized instructions, not real captions, so training the text-CE loss on them risks eroding language ability for no benefit. Collapsing the gpt turn to a constant token makes that loss term contribute nothing informative, leaving the image (flow-matching) loss as the real training signal — this was an explicit requirement for both new runs, not just an artifact of copying the old recipe.
04

Recover the exact SFT recipe used previously

Rather than guess hyperparameters, located and read the actual training script and the actual finished checkpoint from the earlier 100k-row run:

  • Script: Model_Related/InternVLU/InternVL/internvl_chat/shell/internvlu/run_vbvr_gen_sft.sh — LoRA rank 32 on the LLM only (never fully unfrozen), lr 1e-5, effective batch size 16, gen-loss weight 0.5 after a 20-step warmup, all conditioning images through the ViT (the code default, not a flag).
  • Base checkpoint: /scratch/network/ssd2/junlin/models/InternVL-U.
  • Prior 100k-row checkpoint (merged, inference-ready): /scratch/network/ssd/junlin/models/internvlu-vbvr-gen-noce-merged — this is baseline (b)'s starting point.
05

Train both baselines with identical settings

Same script, same META_PATH (the new 4,500-row meta), same hyperparameters for both runs — only INTERNVLU_CKPT and OUTPUT_DIR differ:

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,3 GPUS=2 META_PATH=data/meta/vbvr_target_pred_9task_meta.json OUTPUT_DIR=.../internvlu-vbvr-9task4500-frombase bash shell/internvlu/run_vbvr_gen_sft.sh # (a) from base -- INTERNVLU_CKPT defaults to the base snapshot CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,3 GPUS=2 META_PATH=data/meta/vbvr_target_pred_9task_meta.json OUTPUT_DIR=.../internvlu-vbvr-9task4500-from100k INTERNVLU_CKPT=.../internvlu-vbvr-gen-noce-merged bash shell/internvlu/run_vbvr_gen_sft.sh # (b) continues from the 100k-row checkpoint

GPUs 2,3 on torrnode8 only (not 6,7, which another user's job was lightly using at the time) — the two runs went sequentially, not in parallel, to avoid splitting the 2 free GPUs further. gradient_accumulation_steps is computed as BATCH_SIZE / PER_DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE / GPUS, so dropping from the original 4 GPUs to 2 here automatically doubled it (4→8), preserving the effective batch size of 16 with no config changes needed. EPOCHS was kept at the literal value 1 from the original script (≈282 steps for 4,500 rows) rather than scaled up to match the original run's 6,250 total steps — a deliberate choice to keep every non-data-volume setting identical, not an oversight.

False alarm, not a bug: the first logged step reported ~127s/it (≈10h ETA), which looked alarming. It turned out tqdm's first-iteration timing includes one-time model/data loading overhead; steady state settled to ~28s/step (≈2h10m/run), consistent with the earlier 100k-row run's own trainer_state.json (train_runtime=64,023s / 6,250 steps = 10.24s/step on 4 GPUs → ~2x slower on 2 GPUs is the expected, unremarkable number).
06

Generate on the 900-sample eval split

python inference/run_target_pred_eval.py --gpu <n> --ckpt <merged-pipeline-dir> --tag <name> # --prescale-input defaults to 512 (long-edge resize) -- left at default, matching every other model's runs
1,000 samples were generated, not 900: target_pred_id_eval.jsonl still carries 100 leftover eval rows for shape_outline_then_move, a task dropped from LOCKED_TASKS back on 2026-08-25 for being redundant with another task. run_target_pred_eval.py's load_rows() just reads the whole ID+OOD eval jsonls, so it has no way to know that task isn't active. Harmless (the extra 100 generations/scores per model are simply excluded by this report's hardcoded 9-task list) but worth ~11% extra compute — worth deleting those rows from the source jsonl before the next run.
Node contention doubled inference time, then got fixed mid-run: torrnode8's CPU was saturated by an unrelated user's job (load average ~127 on 64 cores) while its GPUs sat mostly idle, starving this script's CPU-side image preprocessing. Moved both models' inference to less-contended GPUs/nodes (torrnode12, then torrnode8's freed GPU3, then torrnode12 again) once the training GPUs freed up. run_target_pred_eval.py skips any <id>.png that already exists on disk, so killing and relaunching on a different node/GPU loses zero completed samples.
07

Score both models

python validation/score_target_pred_eval.py --run-dir <run_dir> # rule-based, ~3 min for both combined python judge_eval/score_all_with_judge.py --run-dir <run_dir> --workers 8 # judge, ~20 min each, sequential
Judge scoring failed 100% on the first pass (2,000/2,000 "Connection error") — the local vLLM judge server (qwen3-vl-30b-fp8 on localhost:8000) had been shut down that same morning and never restarted; nothing was listening on the port. Recovered the exact original launch invocation from the server's own log file and relaunched it on a free GPU:
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<free gpu> vllm serve /scratch/local/ssd/junlin/models/Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 --trust-remote-code --max-model-len 8192 --enforce-eager --served-model-name qwen3-vl-30b-fp8 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --mm-processor-cache-gb 0.0 --max-num-seqs 4 --port 8000

Re-ran judge scoring for both models against the restarted server: 0 errors, 1,000/1,000 each.

08

Build this report

Adapted from the project's existing 4-model template (artifacts/gen_comparison_report.py) to keep the same visual language and scoring conventions as sibling reports, trimmed to 10 shared examples/task instead of 20 (this phase originally built the 2-model frombase/from100k version; see phase 09 for the from140k addition):

python artifacts/gen_9task_sft_comparison.py # -> artifacts/9task_sft_comparison.html
One fix needed on the way in: the task list can't be taken from TASK_CRITERIA.keys() anymore — it now has 10 entries because shape_outline_then_move was added to it after the historical 900-sample runs. TASK_ORDER here is explicitly the 9 active task names, matching phase 01.
09

Add the from140k model (follow-up session)

Same 4,500-row training set and identical SFT recipe as phases 03-05, but starting from a new, bigger next-frame checkpoint instead of the original 100k one. That checkpoint was itself built first, in the same session:

  • Generated 40,000 fresh next-frame (3-in → 1-out) rows for the 4 tasks that had been held out as OOD in the 100k-row next-frame pretraining set (shape_color_then_move, maze, 2d_geometric_transformation, animal_size_sorting; glass_refraction excluded, still no train jsonl) — raw-video generation first ran sequentially per vbvr_next_frame_generate.py's existing per-task chunking, then was switched mid-run to a task-level-parallel driver (vbvr_next_frame_generate_parallel.py) after a live memory measurement showed a single 500-sample chunk peaks at only ~6GB RSS, making 4 concurrent tasks trivially safe on a 196GB-free shared node.
  • Continuation-SFT'd the existing 100k-row next-frame checkpoint on those 40,000 rows (same run_vbvr_gen_sft.sh, same hyperparameters, only INTERNVLU_CKPT/META_PATH/OUTPUT_DIR changed) — giving a checkpoint that has now seen 100k + 40k = 140,000 next-frame rows total, with the former OOD tasks now treated as ordinary training data rather than held out.
  • Restarted that training run once mid-flight after moving from a node where 3 of 4 GPUs had become contended by other tenants (step time had drifted to ~18s/step) to a node with 4 fully idle A40s (step time then ~11s/step, matching the original 100k run's per-step rate) — save_strategy=no meant the ~2h10m of progress on the contended node was lost and the run restarted from step 0, a deliberate trade given the contended node was actively getting worse, not just occasionally slower.

From there, the same phase-03-through-07 pipeline ran unchanged against this new checkpoint:

OUTPUT_DIR=.../internvlu-vbvr-9task4500-from140k INTERNVLU_CKPT=.../internvlu-vbvr-gen-noce-140k-merged bash shell/internvlu/run_vbvr_gen_sft.sh python inference/run_target_pred_eval.py --gpu <n> --ckpt .../internvlu-vbvr-9task4500-from140k-merged --tag from140k_9task4500 python validation/score_target_pred_eval.py --run-dir results/vbvr_target_pred_eval/from140k_9task4500 python judge_eval/score_all_with_judge.py --run-dir results/vbvr_target_pred_eval/from140k_9task4500 --workers 8 python artifacts/gen_9task_sft_comparison.py # this file, extended: MODELS + a 3rd CSS color/legend/grid-column slot
Judge server needed a restart again: it had been deliberately shut down between sessions to free its GPU. Relaunched with the exact invocation recorded in phase 07 before running judge scoring — 0 errors, 1,000/1,000.
10

Add 10 extra examples for two tasks

On request, maze and 2d_geometric_transformation each got 10 additional shared examples (20 total, up from 10) without touching any other task's samples or perturbing the original 10 for these two tasks: EXTRA_SAMPLES draws the extra picks from an independent per-task RNG stream (random.Random(f"{SEED}:extra:{task}")) seeded and consumed strictly after the original single shared-stream shared_picks computation, excluding ids already picked. Re-running gen_9task_sft_comparison.py after this change reproduces every previously-published sample row byte-for-byte; only new rows are appended.

11

Add a second judge: Qwen3.8-27B, via transformers instead of vLLM

Qwen3.8-27B is a brand-new (released 2026-08-14) hybrid-linear-attention native-VL model. vLLM 0.26.0 already ships native support for its architecture (Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration), but neither checkpoint actually serves on this cluster:

  • The community INT4 quant (cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4, single-GPU) crashes vLLM's Marlin repack CUDA kernel with an empty error message during weight loading. Ruled out a checkpoint/vLLM module-naming mismatch as the cause by directly testing vLLM's hf_to_vllm_mapper against the checkpoint's compressed-tensors ignore-list entries -- the mapping is correct -- so this looks like a bug specific to that third-party quant, not something fixable from the caller side.
  • The official bf16 checkpoint, tensor-parallel=2 across two A40s, gets past NCCL init and weight loading but then hits CUDA error: CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version inside vLLM's vllm_flash_attn extension -- a separately-compiled CUDA-13-targeted binary, bundled unconditionally regardless of which torch+cuXXX variant pip resolves for the main package. --disable-custom-all-reduce routes around an identical CUDA-13 wall in vLLM's custom-all-reduce extension, but --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN does not route around the flash-attn one: that extension gets imported and probed unconditionally at startup regardless of the configured backend.

Also separately root-caused, while investigating whether another node might have a newer driver: the entire cluster (checked 7 of 17 reachable nodes, both A40 and Quadro RTX 6000 boxes) runs the identical Ansible-managed driver, 530.30.02, which supports CUDA up to ~12.8 but not 13 -- so no node on this cluster would serve the bf16 checkpoint via vLLM today.

Plain transformers.generate() sidesteps all of this: attn_implementation="sdpa" uses PyTorch's built-in attention kernel (part of torch itself, not a separately-compiled extension), and the model's own Gated-DeltaNet linear-attention layers have a documented pure-PyTorch fallback. Confirmed working end-to-end (10-run VQA benchmark, 5.6 tok/s average -- much slower than a real vLLM server would give, since this is naive multi-GPU pipeline parallelism with no batching, but it runs) before building evaluators/llm_judge_transformers.py, a drop-in for FullVLMJudge that reuses TASK_CRITERIA/build_full_judge_instruction unchanged and only swaps the OpenAI-client call for a local model.generate() call.

device_map="auto" silently offloads to disk with zero error: accelerate's automatic memory balancer proved too conservative on this box's currently-free GPUs and repeatedly put a few layers (once, just lm_head) on 'disk' rather than erroring -- catastrophic for latency (a first attempt at the VQA benchmark came back at 0.46 tok/s, ~600x slower, purely from repeated disk reads) and gives no warning beyond an easy-to-miss log line. Fix: build the device_map dict by hand (a fixed 40/24 decoder-layer split across the two GPUs used, lm_head/embed_tokens/visual pinned to the fuller one) and assert hf_device_map contains no 'cpu'/'disk' entries before proceeding -- both llm_judge_transformers.py and the benchmark script do this now.
The model's own "low" reasoning-effort setting is not actually short: Qwen3.8-27B's chat template defaults to reasoning_effort="xhigh" and exposes enable_thinking/reasoning_effort template kwargs. Measured reasoning_effort="low" on a 4-criterion task: 238s, and it never even reached the JSON answer within max_tokens=400 -- still produces a long, unstructured visual analysis. enable_thinking=False (template injects an empty <think></think> block, skipping the reasoning step outright) measured at 46s on the identical sample and reliably produces clean, valid JSON with sensible per-criterion reasoning -- used as the default from here on.

Scored the identical shared_picks subset this report already displays (110 ids × 3 models = 330 judge calls), not the full 900/task pool: a real, measured single call is 40–70s (task-criteria-count dependent) even with enable_thinking=False, making the full 2,700-call corpus a ~35–40 hour job -- infeasible in one sitting. User-confirmed scope choice, given both the measured per-call cost and that the ask ("add the new model's score under each visual example") is itself scoped to exactly this subset.

python judge_eval/score_shared_with_qwen38.py # -> results/vbvr_target_pred_eval/<model>_9task4500/judge_scored_qwen38.json (per model, 110 ids each) python artifacts/gen_9task_sft_comparison.py # this file, extended: subset-only 3-way table + section, # qwen3.8 line under every visual example, phase 11

Per-task judge-score ratios between any pair of models aren't baked into this page but are a one-line re-derivation: load two models' judge_scored.json, average judge_score by task_name, divide.

Models: all three InternVL-U, single-image generation, 512px output; only the starting checkpoint and training-data history differ. Judge: qwen3-vl-30b-fp8, temperature 0, images downscaled to 512px on the long edge, one call per sample (900 × 3 = 2,700 total judge calls across this report). Sampling: 10 shared test instances per task (20 for maze and 2d_geometric_transformation, each with 10 extra appended in a follow-up update via an independent RNG stream), Python random.Random(92820260828), identical ids across all three models, not cherry-picked. glass_refraction is excluded: no generations exist for it (its DataFactory generator repo is access-restricted). Second judge (added 2026-08-31): Qwen3.8-27B, bf16, run locally via transformers (attn_implementation="sdpa", enable_thinking=False), temperature 0, same rubric/instruction/weights and same 512px images as the first judge, but scored on only the 110-id shared subset shown on this page (not the full 900/task pool) — see phase 11.
